nodes.name: Orthogonal channel spectrum band
nodes.statement: We consider a spectrum band consisting of $M$ orthogonal channels with identical bandwidth~\cite{Jia08,Hu11MC}.

nodes.name: Channels allocated to K primary networks
nodes.statement: We assume that the $M$ channels are allocated to $K$ primary networks, which cover different service areas.

nodes.name: Markov channel occupancy
nodes.statement: Due to primary user transmissions, the occupancy of each channel evolves following a discrete-time Markov process, as validated by recent measurement studies~\cite{Zhao07a, Su08, Motamedi07}.
nodes.statement_short: Each channel's occupancy follows a discrete-time Markov process.

nodes.name: Channel status
nodes.statement: In primary network $k$, the status of channel $m$ in time slot $t$ is denoted by $S_m^k(t)$ with idle (i.e., $S_m^k(t)=0$) and busy (i.e., $S_m^k(t)=1$) states.

nodes.name: Channel transition probabilities
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda_m^k$ and $\mu_m^k$ be the transition probability of remaining in state $0$ and that from state $1$ to $0$, respectively, for channel $m$ in primary network $k$.

nodes.name: Channel utilization
nodes.statement: The utilization of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, denoted by $\eta_m^k = \Pr(S_m^k=1)$, is \begin{eqnarray} \eta_m^k = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \mbox{$\sum_{t=1}^T$} S_m^k(t) = \frac{1-\lambda_m^k}{1-\lambda_m^k+\mu_m^k}. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Utilization $\eta_m^k$ is the stationary busy probability of the two-state Markov chain.

nodes.name: Stationary busy probability of a channel
nodes.statement: \eta_m^k = \lim_{T \to \infty} \frac{1}{T} \mbox{$\sum_{t=1}^T$} S_m^k(t) = \frac{1-\lambda_m^k}{1-\lambda_m^k+\mu_m^k}.
nodes.label: eq:ProbBusy1

nodes.name: Multicast groups
nodes.statement: As shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:ntwarch}, we consider a CR base station multicasts $G$ real-time videos to $G$ multicast groups, each of which have $N_g$ users, $g=1, 2, \cdots, G$.

nodes.name: Tile
nodes.statement: Note that a time slot and channel combination, termed a {\em tile}, is the minimum unit for resource allocation.
nodes.genus: a time slot and channel combination
differentia: the minimum unit for resource allocation

nodes.name: CR nodes in coverage of primary network k
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{U}^k$ denote the set of CR nodes that are located within the coverage of primary network $k$.

nodes.name: Video session source and destination
nodes.statement: A video session $l$ may be relayed by multiple CR nodes if source $z_l$ is not a one-hop neighbor of destination $d_l$.

nodes.name: Common control channel
nodes.statement: We assume a {\em common control channel} for the CR network~\cite{Su08}.

nodes.name: Control channel timescale
nodes.statement: We also assume the timescale of the primary channel process (or, the time slot durations) is much larger than the broadcast delays on the control channel, such that feedbacks of channel information can be received at the source nodes in a timely manner.

nodes.name: Virtual tunnel
nodes.statement: In the transmission phase, the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path form a virtual ``tunnel'' connecting source $z_l$ and destination $d_l$.
nodes.genus: the channels assigned to a video session $l$ at each link along the path

nodes.name: Amplify-and-forward transmission
nodes.statement: We adopt amplify-and-forward for video transmission~\cite{Laneman04}.

nodes.name: False alarm and miss detection
nodes.statement: A {\em false alarm} may lead to waste a spectrum opportunity and a {\em miss detection} may causes collision with primary users.

nodes.name: Channel hypotheses
nodes.statement: Denote $H_0$ as the hypothesis that channel $m$ in primary network $k$ is idle, and $H_1$ the hypothesis that channel $m$ in primary network $k$ is busy in time slot $t$.

nodes.name: Channel availability belief
nodes.statement: The conditional probability that channel $m$ is available in primary network $k$, denoted by $a_m^k(t)$, can be derived as, \begin{eqnarray} a_m^k(t) &=& \Pr(H_0|W_i^m=\theta_i^m, \; i \in \mathcal{U}_m^k, \pi_m^k) \nonumber \\ &=& \left[ 1 + \left( \varphi_m^k \right)^{u_m^k} \left( \phi_m^k \right)^{|\mathcal{U}_m^k|-u_m^k} \frac{\Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k)}{\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k)} \right]^{-1}. \end{eqnarray} where $\theta_i^m$ represents a specific sensing result (0 or 1), $\mathcal{U}_m^k$ is the subset of users in $\mathcal{U}^k$ (i.e., the set of CR nodes that are located within the coverage of primary network $k$) that sense channel $m$, $u_m^k$ is the number of users in $\mathcal{U}_m^k$ observing channel $m$ is idle, $\pi_m^k$ represents the history of channel $m$ in primary network $k$, and $\varphi_m^k$ and $\phi_m^k$ are defined as: \begin{eqnarray} \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=0|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=0|H_0)}=\frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=0 \\ \phi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=1|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=1|H_0)}=\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=1 . \end{array}\right. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Posterior probability $a_m^k(t)$ that a channel is idle given cooperative sensing results and channel history, with likelihood ratios $\varphi,\phi$ from false-alarm/miss-detection rates.

nodes.name: Posterior channel availability
nodes.statement: a_m^k(t) &=& \Pr(H_0|W_i^m=\theta_i^m, \; i \in \mathcal{U}_m^k, \pi_m^k) \nonumber \\ &=& \left[ 1 + \left( \varphi_m^k \right)^{u_m^k} \left( \phi_m^k \right)^{|\mathcal{U}_m^k|-u_m^k} \frac{\Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k)}{\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k)} \right]^{-1}.
nodes.label: eq:AvailProb1

nodes.name: Sensing likelihood ratios
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} \varphi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=0|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=0|H_0)}=\frac{\delta_m}{1-\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=0 \\ \phi_m^k=\frac{P(W_i^m=1|H_1)}{P(W_i^m=1|H_0)}=\frac{1-\delta_m}{\epsilon_m}, & \mbox{when } \theta_i^m=1 . \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq:DefVarPhi

nodes.name: One-step channel prediction
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k) = \lambda_m^k a_m^k(t-1) + \mu_m^k \left[ 1-a_m^k(t-1) \right] \\ \Pr(H_1|\pi_m^k) = 1-\Pr(H_0|\pi_m^k). \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:OneStep

nodes.name: Base and enhancement layer rates
nodes.statement: With FGS or MGS coding, each video $l$ is encoded into one base layer with rate $R_l^b$ and one enhancement layer with rate $R_l^e$.

nodes.name: Total video bit rate
nodes.statement: The total bit rate for video $l$ is $R_l=R_l^b+R_l^e$.

nodes.name: Linear rate-PSNR model
nodes.statement: As in prior work~\cite{Schaar03}, the average PSNR of video $l$, denoted as $Q_l$, can be estimated as: \begin{equation} Q_l(R_l) = Q_l^b + \beta_l(R_l - R_l^b) = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l, \end{equation} where $Q_l^b$ is the resulting PSNR when the base layer is decoded alone, $\beta_l$ a constant depending on the video sequence and codec setting, and $Q_l^0 = Q_l^b - \beta_l R_l^b$.
nodes.statement_short: Average PSNR of video $l$ is modeled as affine in its rate, $Q_l = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l$.

nodes.name: Rate-distortion model
nodes.statement: Q_l(R_l) = Q_l^b + \beta_l(R_l - R_l^b) = Q_l^0 + \beta_l R_l,
nodes.label: eq:RDfun

nodes.name: GOP delivery deadline
nodes.statement: Due to the real-time nature, we assume that each {\em group of pictures} (GOP) must be delivered during the next GOP window, which consists of $N_G$ time slots.

nodes.name: Maximum collision and transmission probabilities
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma_n \in (0, 1)$ be the {\em maximum allowed collision probability} with primary users on channel $n$, and $p^{tr}_n(t)$ the {\em transmission probability} on channel $n$ for the base station in time slot $t$.

nodes.name: Primary user collision constraint
nodes.statement: The probability of collision caused by the base station should be kept below $\gamma_n$, i.e., $p^{tr}_n(t) \left[ 1 - a_n(t) \right] \le \gamma_n$.

nodes.name: Opportunistic transmission probability
nodes.statement: p^{tr}_n(t) = \left\{ \begin{array} {ll} \min \left\{ 1, \frac{\gamma_n}{1-a_n(t)} \right\}, & \mbox{ if }\; 0 \leq a_n(t) < 1 \\ 1, & \mbox{ if }\; a_n(t) =1. \end{array} \right.
nodes.label: eq:ptran

nodes.name: Modulation-Coding schemes
nodes.statement: We consider $M$ unique combinations of modulation and FEC schemes, termed {\em Modulation-Coding} (MC) schemes, in this paper.

nodes.name: Ordered list of MC schemes
nodes.statement: Let $\{MC_m\}_{m=1,\cdots,M}$ be the list of available MC schemes indexed according to their data rates in the increasing order.

nodes.name: Slow fading channels
nodes.statement: We assume slow fading channels with coherence time larger than a time slot.

nodes.name: Users decoding each MC scheme
nodes.statement: At the beginning of a time slot, the base station is able to collect the number $n_{g,m}$ of users in each multicast group $g$ who can successfully decode $MC_m$ signals for $m=1, 2, \cdots, M$.

nodes.name: Base layer uses MC_1
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we assume that the base layer is always transmitted using $MC_1$.

nodes.name: Enhancement sub-layers
nodes.statement: We further divide the enhancement layer into $M$ sub-layers, where sub-layer $m$ has rate $R_{g,m}^e$ and uses $MC_m$.

nodes.name: Tiles per sub-layer
nodes.statement: Assuming that $MC_m$ can carry $b_{g,m}$ bits of video $g$ in one tile, we denote the number of tiles for sub-layer $m$ of video $g$ as $l_{g,m} \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Enhancement layer rate as sum over sub-layers
nodes.statement: R_g^e = \sum_{m=1}^M R_{g,m}^e = \sum_{m=1}^M b_{g,m} l_{g,m}.

nodes.name: User utility
nodes.statement: Since we consider video quality in this paper, we define the utility for user $i$ in group $g$ as $U_{g,i} = \log Q_{g,i} = \log \left( Q^b_g+\beta_g R^e_g(i) \right)$, where $R^e_g(i)$ is the received enhancement layer rate of user $i$ in group $g$.

nodes.name: Group utility
nodes.statement: The total utility for group $g$ is $U_g = \sum_{i=1}^{N_g} U_{g,i}$.

nodes.name: Group utility by MC classes
nodes.statement: U_g = \sum_{k=1}^M(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1})\log \left( Q^b_g+\beta_g \sum_{m=1}^k R_{g,m}^e \right),

nodes.name: System utility
nodes.statement: The utility function of the entire CR video multicast system is \begin{equation} U = \sum_{g=1}^G U_g. \end{equation}

nodes.name: System utility
nodes.statement: U = \sum_{g=1}^G U_g.

nodes.name: Proportional fairness of utility maximization
nodes.statement: Maximizing $U$ will achieve {\em proportional fairness} among the video sessions~\cite{Kelly98}

nodes.name: Base and maximal enhancement layer rates
nodes.statement: To address heterogeneous user channels, we adopt FGS to produce a base layer with rate $R^b_g$ and an enhancement layer with rate $\bar{R}_g^e$.

nodes.name: Effective rate
nodes.statement: During transmission, we determine the {\em effective rate} for each enhancement layer $R_g^e \leq \bar{R}^e_g$ depending on channel availability, sensing, and MC schemes.

nodes.name: Opportunistic spectrum access and transmission
nodes.statement: In each time slot $t$, the base station opportunistically access every channel $n$ with probability $p_n^{tr}(t)$ given in (\ref{eq:ptran}). Specifically, for each channel $n$, the base station generates a random number $x_n(t)$, which is independent of the channel history $\theta_n(t)$ and uniformly distributed in [0,1]. If $x_n(t) \leq p_n^{tr}(t)$, the most important packet among those not ACKed in the previous GoP will be transmitted on channel $n$. If an ACK is received for this packet at the end of time slot $t$, this packet is successfully received by at least one of the users and will be removed from the transmission buffer. Otherwise, there is a collision with primary user and this packet will remain in the transmission buffer and will be retransmitted.
nodes.statement_short: Per slot and channel, transmit the most important un-ACKed packet with probability $p_n^{tr}(t)$; drop it on ACK, else keep for retransmission.

nodes.name: Draw random number
nodes.statement: Specifically, for each channel $n$, the base station generates a random number $x_n(t)$, which is independent of the channel history $\theta_n(t)$ and uniformly distributed in [0,1].

nodes.name: Transmit if below threshold
nodes.statement: If $x_n(t) \leq p_n^{tr}(t)$, the most important packet among those not ACKed in the previous GoP will be transmitted on channel $n$.

nodes.name: Remove ACKed packet
nodes.statement: If an ACK is received for this packet at the end of time slot $t$, this packet is successfully received by at least one of the users and will be removed from the transmission buffer.

nodes.name: Keep collided packet
nodes.statement: Otherwise, there is a collision with primary user and this packet will remain in the transmission buffer and will be retransmitted.

nodes.name: Known number of enhancement tiles
nodes.statement: We assume that the number of tiles used for the enhancement layers in a GoP window, $T_e$, is known at the beginning of the GoP window.
nodes.section: 4.2.2 Enhancement Layer Partitioning and Tile Allocation

nodes.name: OPT-Part
nodes.statement: Letting $\vec{l} = [l_{1,1}, l_{1,2}, \cdots, l_{1,M}, l_{2,1}, \cdots l_{G,M}]$ denote the {\em tile allocation vector}, we formulate an optimization problem OPT-Part as follows. \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} U(\vec{l}) = \sum_{g=1}^{G}\sum_{k=1}^M(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) \times \log \left[ Q^b_g+\beta_g \sum_{m=1}^k b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \right] \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{g=1}^G\sum_{m=1}^M l_{g,m}\le T_e \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} \sum_{m=1}^M b_{g,m}l_{g,m} \le \bar{R}_g^e, \; g \in [1, \cdots, M] \\ && \hspace*{-0.2in} l_{g,m} \geq 0, \; m \in [1, \cdots, M], g \in [1, \cdots, G]. \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Choose tile allocations $l_{g,m}$ maximizing proportional-fair video utility subject to tile budget $T_e$ and maximum enhancement rates.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
(i) {\em Complexity}: In Step 4 in Table~ef{tab:GreedyAlgo1}, it takes $O(MG)$ to solve for $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}$. Since each iteration assigns one tile to sub-layer $\hat{m}$ of group $\hat{g}$, it takes $T_e$ iterations to allocate all the available tiles in a GoP window. Therefore, the overall complexity of GRD1 is $O(MGT_e)$. (ii) {\em Optimality Bound}: This proof is extended from a result first shown in~\cite{Deb08} for layered videos. We first show a property of group utility $U_g(\vec{l})$, which will be used in the proof of the optimality gap. For two vectors $\vec{l}^1_g$ and $\vec{l}^2_g$, letting $\Delta = U_g(\vec{l}^1_g)-U_g(\vec{l}^2_g)$, we have  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.2in} \Delta = \sum_{k=1}^M (n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  rac{ \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m}(l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2) }{ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 } ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^k (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1+  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g+\sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.2in} \le \sum_{k=1}^M \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+(n_{g,k}-n_{g,k+1}) 	imes \log \left( 1 +  eta_g b_{g,m} / \left[ Q^b_g + \sum_{m=1}^k  eta_g b_{g,m} l_{g,m}^2 ight] ight) 
onumber\ & & \hspace{-0.2in} = \sum_{m=1}^M (l_{g,m}^1-l_{g,m}^2)^+ \left[ U_g(\vec{l}^2_g+b_{g,m})-U(\vec{l}^2_g) ight], \end{eqnarray} where $y^+=\max \{ 0, y \}$. The first inequality is due to the concavity of logarithm functions. Next we prove the optimality bound. Let $\vec{l}_{t}$ be the output of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. Let the utility gap between the optimal solution and the GRD1 solution be $F_{t} = U(\vec{l}^{\ast}) - U(\vec{l}_{t})$, and $\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)$ the argument found in Step 4 of GRD1 after $t$ iterations. We have $\vec{l}_{t} = \vec{l}_{t-1} + \vec{e}_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)$ and  egin{eqnarray} & & \hspace{-0.1in} F_{t-1} = U(\vec{l}^{\ast})-U(\vec{l}_{t-1}) 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{g,m}(t))-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})] 
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le \sum_g\sum_m (l_{g,m}^{\ast}-l_{g,m})^{+} [U(\vec{l}_{t-1}+\vec{e}_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t))- U(\vec{l}_{t-1})]  rac{b_{g,m}+R/T_e}{b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}
onumber \ & & \hspace{-0.3in} \le  rac{U(\vec{l}_t)-U(\vec{l}_{t-1})}{ b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t) + R/T_e} \sum_g\sum_m [l_{g,m}^{\ast}(b_{g,m}+R/T_e)]. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The first inequality is due to (ef{eq:lema2}) and the second inequality follows Step 4 of GRD1. It follows (ef{eq:st1}) that $\sum_g\sum_m l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le T_e$ and $\sum_g\sum_m b_{g,m}l_{g,m}^{\ast} \le R$. We have $F_{t-1} \le (F_{t-1}-F_{t})  rac{2R}{b_{\hat{g}, \hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e}$. Solving for $F_t$, we have $F_{t}\le F_{t-1} \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\}$. Suppose the {\em WHILE} loop in Table~ef{tab:GreedyAlgo1} has been executed $k$ times when the solution is obtained.  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_{k-1} \left\{ 1-\left[b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(k)+R/T_eight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \prod_{t=1}^k \left\{ 1 - \left[ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ight] / (2R) ight\} 
onumber \ &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} The {\em WHILE} loop exits when one or both of two constraints are violated. If $\sum_{g}\sum_{m} l_{g,m} \le T_e$ is violated, there is no tile that can be used. Therefore $k \ge T_e$ and $\sum_{t=1}^kR/T_e\ge R$. If constraint ``$A$ is not empty'' is violated, all the videos have been allocated sufficient number of tiles and will be transmitted at full rates. We have $\sum_{t=1}^k b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t) \geq R$ in this case. It follows that  egin{eqnarray} F_k &\le& F_0 \left\{ 1 - 1/(2kR) \sum_{t=1}^k [ b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t)+R/T_e ] ight\}^k 
onumber \ & \le & F_0 \left[ 1 - 1/(2k) ight]^k \; \le \; F_0 e^{-1/2}. 
onumber \end{eqnarray} Since $F_0=U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$, we have $U(\vec{l}_k)\ge(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$. Therefore, we conclude that the GRD1 solution is bounded by $(1-e^{-1/2})U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$ and $U(\vec{l}^{\ast})$.

nodes.name: Loop exit cases
nodes.statement: The {\em WHILE} loop exits when one or both of two constraints are violated. If $\sum_{g}\sum_{m} l_{g,m} \le T_e$ is violated, there is no tile that can be used. Therefore $k \ge T_e$ and $\sum_{t=1}^kR/T_e\ge R$. If constraint ``$A$ is not empty'' is violated, all the videos have been allocated sufficient number of tiles and will be transmitted at full rates. We have $\sum_{t=1}^k b_{\hat{g},\hat{m}}(t) \geq R$ in this case.
nodes.statement_short: In both exit cases the per-step increments sum to at least $R$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: Suppose there exists a pair of $i$ and $j$ where $\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) > \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)$ and $c_i(t) < c_j(t)$. We can further increase E[Reward] by switching the tile assignment, i.e., assign channel $i$ to $\xi_j$ and channel $j$ to $\xi_i$. With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray} Therefore E[Reward] is maximized when the $\{ \mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) \}$ and $\{c_i(t)\}$ are in the same order.
nodes.statement_short: Exchange argument: swapping a mis-ordered pair strictly increases expected reward.

With this new assignment, the net increase in E[Reward] is \begin{eqnarray} & & \hspace*{-0.3in} c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) + c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)-c_i(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i)-c_j(t)\mbox{Inc}(\xi_j) \nonumber \\ & = & [c_j(t) - c_i(t)][\mbox{Inc}(\xi_i) - \mbox{Inc}(\xi_j)] > 0. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Optimal channel-to-tunnel assignment at a relay
nodes.statement: Consider three consecutive nodes along a path, denoted as nodes $i$, $j$, and $k$. Idle channels 1 and 2 are available at link $\{i, j\}$ and idle channels 3 and 4 are available at link $\{j, k\}$. Assume the packet loss rates of the four channels satisfy $p_{i,j}^1 > p_{i,j}^2$ and $p_{j,k}^3 > p_{j,k}^4$. To set up two tunnels, assigning channels \{1, 3\} to one tunnel and channels \{2, 4\} to the other tunnel achieves the maximum expectation of successful transmission on path section $\{i, j, k\}$.

nodes.name: OPT-rPS relaxed path selection
nodes.statement: To solve Problem OPT-PS, we first relax binary variables $y_l^h$ to allow them take real values in [0,1] and obtain the following {\em relaxed path selection} problem (OPT-rPS): \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h\in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: LP relaxation of OPT-PS with $y_l^h\in[0,1]$.

nodes.name: OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: \mbox{maximize:} && f(\mathbf{y}) = \sum_l \sum_h F_l^h y_l^h \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \sum_l\sum_{h\in \mathcal{P}_l} w_{l,h}^g y_l^h \le 1, \; \mbox{for all } \; g \nonumber \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l. \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:rPathSelec

nodes.name: Lagrangian of OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: We then introduce positive Lagrange Multipliers $e_g$ for the path selection constraints in Problem OPT-rPS and obtain the corresponding {\em Lagrangian function}: \begin{eqnarray} && \hspace{-0.45in} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h F_l^h y_l^h + \sum_g e_g (1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h ( F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g ) + \sum_g e_g \nonumber \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h ( y_l^h, \mathbf{e} )+ \sum_g e_g. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Lagrangian relaxing the path constraints with multipliers $e_g$, separable over paths.

nodes.name: Lagrangian function
nodes.statement: && \hspace{-0.45in} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h F_l^h y_l^h + \sum_g e_g (1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h ( F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g ) + \sum_g e_g \nonumber \\ && = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h ( y_l^h, \mathbf{e} )+ \sum_g e_g. \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:LagFun

nodes.name: Lower-level per-path subproblem
nodes.statement: At the lower level, we have the following subproblems, one for each path $\mathcal{P}_l^h$, \begin{eqnarray} \max_{0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1} \mathcal{L}_l^h(y_l^h, \mathbf{e})=F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g. \end{eqnarray}

nodes.name: Lower-level subproblem
nodes.statement: \max_{0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1} \mathcal{L}_l^h(y_l^h, \mathbf{e})=F_l^hy_l^h - \sum_g w_{l,h}^g y_l^h e_g.
nodes.label: eq:FirstLevel

nodes.name: Relaxed dual problem
nodes.statement: At the higher level, by updating the dual variables $e_g$, we can solve the {\em relaxed dual problem}: \begin{eqnarray} \min_{\mathbf{e} \ge 0} \;\; q(\mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h \left( \left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}, \mathbf{e} \right) + \sum_g e_g, \end{eqnarray} where $\left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}$ is the optimal solution to (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}).

nodes.name: Relaxed dual problem
nodes.statement: \min_{\mathbf{e} \ge 0} \;\; q(\mathbf{e}) = \sum_l\sum_h \mathcal{L}_l^h \left( \left( y_l^h \right)^{\ast}, \mathbf{e} \right) + \sum_g e_g,
nodes.label: eq:SecondLevel

nodes.name: Subgradient method
nodes.statement: Since the solution to (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}) is unique, the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) can be solved using the following {\em subgradient method} that iteratively updates the Lagrange Multipliers~\cite{Bertsekas99}: \begin{eqnarray} e_g(\tau+1) = \left[ e_g(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)(1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \right]^+, \end{eqnarray} where $\tau$ is the iteration index, $\alpha(\tau)$ is a sufficiently small positive step size and $[x]^+$ denotes $\max\{x, 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Projected subgradient update of the Lagrange multipliers $e_g$.

nodes.name: Subgradient multiplier update
nodes.statement: e_g(\tau+1) = \left[ e_g(\tau)-\alpha(\tau)(1 - \sum_l\sum_h w_{l,h}^g y_l^h) \right]^+,
nodes.label: eq:SubGrad

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: According to Fact~\ref{thm:EqualCont}, the linearized problem of OPT-PS, i.e., OPT-rPS, can be rewritten as an equality constrained problem in the following form: \begin{eqnarray} \mbox{maximize:} && \mathbf{F}'\mathbf{y} \\ \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} where $\mathbf{F}$, $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, and $\mathbf{y}$ are column vectors with elements $F_l^h$, $w_{l,h}^g$, and $y_l^h$, respectively. We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation} Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible. Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation} Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value. Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite OPT-rPS with active constraints as equalities, Gauss-Jordan eliminate to express dependent variables as integer combinations of free ones, then optimize the free binaries.

nodes.statement: \mbox{subject to:} && \mathbf{w}_j' \mathbf{y}=1, \;\; j \in \mathcal{A}(\mathbf{y}^{\ast}) \\ && 0 \leq y_l^h \leq 1, \; \mbox{for all } h,l, \nonumber
nodes.label: eq:EqualCons1

nodes.name: Gauss-Jordan elimination
nodes.statement: We apply {\em Gauss-Jordan elimination} to the constraints in (\ref{eq:EqualCons1}) to solve for $\mathbf{y}$. Since there is not sufficient number of equations, some $y_l^h$'s are free variables (denoted as $y_i^f$) and the rest are dependent variables (denoted as $y_j^d$). Assuming there are $r$ free variables, the dependent variables can be written as linear combinations of the free variables after Gauss-Jordan elimination, as \begin{equation} y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Express dependent variables via free ones.

nodes.name: Dependent variables as combinations of free ones
nodes.statement: y_j^d = \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{w}_j^i y_i^f + \bar{b}_j, \; j \in \mathcal{A}(y_i^{\ast}).
nodes.label: eq:depdent

nodes.name: Integrality and feasibility
nodes.statement: Due to Gauss-Jordan elimination and binary vectors $\mathbf{w}_j$'s, $\bar{w}_j^i$ and $\bar{b}_j$ in (\ref{eq:depdent}) are all integers. Therefore, if all the free variables $y_i^f$ attain binary values, then all the dependent variables $y_j^d$ computed using (\ref{eq:depdent}) will also be integers. Since $0 \leq y_j^d \leq 1$, being integers means that they are either 0 or 1, i.e., binaries. That is, such a solution will be feasible.
nodes.statement_short: Integer coefficients make binary free variables give binary dependent ones: feasibility.

nodes.name: Eliminate dependent variables
nodes.statement: Next we substitute (\ref{eq:depdent}) into problem (\ref{eq:EqualCons}) to eliminate all the dependent variables. Then we obtain a unconstrained problem with only $r$ free variables, as \begin{equation} \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0 \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an unconstrained problem in the free variables.

nodes.name: Reduced unconstrained problem
nodes.statement: \mbox{maximize:} \;\; \sum_{i=1}^r \bar{F}_i y_i^f + \bar{b}_0
nodes.label: eq:GaussElimi

nodes.name: Optimize free variables
nodes.statement: Since the free variables $y_i^f$'s take value in \{0, 1\}, this problem can be easily solved as follows. If the coefficient $\bar{F}_i > 0$, we set $y_i^f=1$; otherwise, if $\bar{F}_i < 0$, we set $y_i^f=0$. Thus (\ref{eq:GaussElimi}) achieves its maximum objective value.
nodes.statement_short: Set each free variable by the sign of its coefficient.

nodes.name: Conclude optimal feasible solution
nodes.statement: Once all the free variables are determined with their optimal binary values, we computes the dependent variables using (\ref{eq:depdent}), which are also binary as discussed above. Thus we obtain a feasible solution, which is optimal.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting binary solution is feasible and optimal.

nodes.name: Strong duality for OPT-rPS
nodes.statement: If the relaxed primal Problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec}) has an optimal solution, then the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) also has an optimal solution and the corresponding optimal values of the two problems are identical.
assumptions: the relaxed primal Problem OPT-rPS in (\ref{eq:rPathSelec}) has an optimal solution
conclusions: the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) also has an optimal solution and the corresponding optimal values of the two problems are identical

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: By definition, the problems in (\ref{eq:LagFun}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) are primal/dual problems. The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution. We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: LP duality: the bounded LP primal has an optimum, so the dual does, and strong duality holds for LPs.

nodes.name: Primal/dual pair

nodes.statement_short: Identify the primal/dual pair.

nodes.name: Dual has optimum
nodes.statement: The primal problem always has an optimal solution because it is bounded. Since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem, the relaxed dual problem is also bounded and feasible. Therefore the relaxed dual problem also has an optimal solution.
nodes.statement_short: Boundedness of the LP gives an optimal dual solution.

nodes.name: Strong duality
nodes.statement: We have the {\em strong duality} if the primal problem is convex, which is the case here since Problem OPT-rPS is an LP problem.
nodes.statement_short: Strong duality holds since OPT-rPS is an LP.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement: We have Theorem~\ref{th:th2} on the optimality of the path selection solution, which follows naturally from Lemmas~\ref{lemma:1} and~\ref{lemma:2}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 1 (integrality of the relaxation) and Lemma 2 (strong duality).

nodes.statement: The optimal solution to the relaxed dual problem (\ref{eq:FirstLevel}) and (\ref{eq:SecondLevel}) is also feasible and optimal to the original path selection Problem OPT-PS given in (\ref{eq:PathSelec}).

nodes.name: Perfect control channel
nodes.statement: We assume a perfect control channel such that channel information can be effectively distributed and shared, which is not confined by the time slot structure~\cite{Su08}.

nodes.name: Large primary slot timescale
nodes.statement: We assume relatively large timescales for the primary network time slots, and small to medium diameter for the CR network, such that there is sufficient time for timely feedback of channel information to the video source nodes and for the distributed algorithms to converge.
